[1] The summer I was fifteen my mother put me on the eastbound bus with a duffel and a jar of her pickled plums and sent me to my aunt Ceno, who had eleven acres of apple trees above the river and nobody left to help her work them. It was the third dry year. I understood that I was being given away for ten weeks, and I understood, dimly, that I was also being given something, though at the time I could not have said what it was, and I spent the ride composing the letter of complaint I meant to send home and never sent.

[2] Ceno grafted. The orchard she had inherited was ninety years old in places; the trunks of those trees were as thick as barrels and sound all the way through, and they bore a fruit that no packing house in the valley would take at any price. So every spring she cut scions from the varieties the buyers did want and set them into the old wood. It is the cheapest thing in farming. A new block on dwarfing stock costs money and five years; a scion costs a knife.

[3] I wanted to know within the week whether mine had worked. Ceno said the same sentence to me so many times that summer that I can still hear the flatness she said it in: a graft takes or it does not, and the tree will tell you in August, not in May. She was not consoling me. She was declining to guess, and she declined in exactly the same tone whether the question was mine or her own, which I took for indifference and which was not indifference at all.

[4] In the second week I carried a scion up from the bundle in the cellar, walked out to the tree at the fence line that Ceno had written off as too far gone to bother with, and made my own graft there without telling her. I wrapped it badly, I think. I told myself I kept it to myself because she would have said the tree was not worth the wood. The truer reason was that a thing nobody knows about cannot be a thing you failed at.

[5] Once a fortnight Mr. Baradas drove up from the valley to buy what there was to buy, and each time he told my aunt that the sensible course was to pull the old trees out and put in young ones, and each time she poured him coffee and let him finish. I wrote him down in my head as the enemy. He was not the enemy. He was a careful man making the argument a careful man would make about ninety-year-old trees in a drought, and my aunt never once said he was wrong; she said only that he was costing the orchard out at the price of one season's fruit, and that she had a different figure in mind.

[6] What she did instead of arguing was keep the ledger. Every graft she set went into it - the date, the tree, the variety of the scion, and in August a mark for took or did not take. Her notes were spare; a whole row of them would not have filled a postcard. And yet out of those columns you could read the history of the place, which years had been kind and which variety would not hold on that rootstock no matter how the season went. She had eleven years of it in the book. When Mr. Baradas talked about young trees she never mentioned the ledger to him, which I did not understand then and do understand now.

[7] In August she took me down the rows with a knife. My graft at the fence line was dead. She cut the wrap off it and showed me why, and the why was not the wrap and not the tree. The two cut faces had been set a quarter inch out of true, so that the green layer under the bark of the one had never touched the green layer under the bark of the other, and the scion had spent four months drawing on a supply that was not there. Two of her own had gone the same way that year, she said, and she said it in the voice of a woman naming the weather.

[8] Then she entered mine in the ledger. Date, tree, variety, a mark in the August column - and beside it, in the margin where she put nothing at all for her own rows, my initials. I have thought about that margin for thirty years. She was not being gentle with me and she was not keeping score against me. She was doing to my failure the one thing she did to her own, which was to turn it into a line that somebody could count later, and the initials were there because a line you can trace to a hand is worth more than a line you cannot. Now you have a record, she said, and not a memory.

[9] I have eight acres of my own now, on worse ground, and I keep the book. What I had wrong at fifteen was not the grafting; the thumbnail work came to me by the second summer, as it comes to anybody who does enough of it. What I had wrong was the size of the unit. I thought the question was whether the graft I had made that morning would live. It was a real question and it was the wrong one to be standing in the row asking. Ceno was not waiting for August out of patience. She was waiting for the eleventh August and then the twelfth, because one graft tells you nothing and four hundred tell you what to plant.

prompt: The second paragraph credits Ceno's grafting with two separate advantages. They are that it:
choices: keeps the old root systems, which a dry year makes worth more than young ones, and puts the new fruit into bearing a season sooner than a block would.
saves the ninety-year-old trees from a clearance the drought would otherwise have forced, and keeps the orchard at its full acreage.
spreads the risk of a bad season across several varieties, and can be repeated each spring for the cost of the cutting.
puts the buyers' varieties on wood that is still sound, and does it without the money and the years a new block costs.
correct_answer: puts the buyers' varieties on wood that is still sound, and does it without the money and the years a new block costs.

[1] Four lines of Ilka Demeter's "Field, November" have been turned into English three times in a century, by translators who agreed on almost nothing, and a reader who sets the versions side by side notices first that they are not even the same size. Fane's 1912 quatrain runs to thirty-eight syllables. Aird's 1968 version runs to twenty-six and breaks into five lines. Ozias, in 2004, gives twenty-nine across four. None of the three is careless. No two of them are wrong in the same place.

[2] The Hungarian is a strict little machine. Demeter is working in a nine-syllable measure she used nowhere else, and she ends her second and fourth lines on der and kenyer - frost and bread - which rhyme fully, and which in the idiom of her region are also the two halves of a proverb about a hard winter. The rhyme is therefore not decoration. It is the poem's argument, compressed into a sound, and a translator who gives up the rhyme gives up the claim.

[3] Fane kept it. He gave himself hoar and store, pulled the syntax around into an inversion no English speaker has produced since, and delivered a quatrain that rhymes, scans, and sounds like a hymnal. It is easy, and it has become customary, to be condescending about this version. But Fane is the only one of the three who registers that the poem is built on a sound, and the stiffness of his English is the price of a structural fact the other two let go. What he paid it with was the ordinary voice. Demeter's diction in the Hungarian is flat, domestic, almost without literary furniture; Fane's is furniture throughout.

[4] Aird, writing at the height of the vogue for plainness, produced what most anthologies still print. She recovered the ordinary voice exactly - in her hands the poem sounds like a woman saying something across a kitchen table - and she recovered it by letting the rhyme go, and the nine-syllable measure with it, and the proverb that lived inside the rhyme. That is a trade and not an oversight. Aird knew what was in those two words; she says so in a letter to her editor, and she says she could not have both.

[5] Ozias tried to hold both and had to pay somewhere else. He found an English pair, rime and crust, that carries the frost and the bread and is idiomatic enough not to creak; and to get those two words into rhyming position he compressed his third line until a clause fell out of it, the clause in which Demeter calls the field idegen, a stranger. Word for word, the Ozias version is the least complete of the three. Everything he preserved was bought with that missing clause, and he prints the Hungarian underneath so that the purchase can be seen.

[6] Talk about translation goes wrong, I think, at the point where it pictures a poem crossing from one language into another and arriving with some percentage of itself intact. The traffic between two languages is not carriage. It is negotiation, and every version is a settlement with terms. Fane's terms are rhyme over voice. Aird's are voice over structure. Ozias pays in clauses. These are not three attempts at one target with three error rates; they are three different bargains, and a reader is owed the terms of the one in front of her.

[7] There is a fact that ought to embarrass anyone who wants to rank the three by fidelity, and it is that Demeter was herself a translator. Her Hungarian versions of the French poet Aline Ricour, published in 1934, are not faithful by any standard she would have been graded on. She moves stanzas. She supplies an image where the French has an abstraction. In one poem she changes the season. And in the note that prefaces the book she writes that she had tried to make in Hungarian the thing Ricour had made in French, and that doing so had obliged her to write different words. She did not take herself to be approximating an object. She took herself to be building a second one.

[8] The strongest case against all of this comes from the reader with no Hungarian, which is nearly every reader, and who quite reasonably wants a poem rather than a seminar on what a poem could not become. That reader is owed something whole, and I concede the priority: a version that does not work as an English poem has failed before any of the interesting questions arise, and Fane's, whatever it preserves, is now read for pleasure by almost nobody. But the concession settles less than it appears to settle. It tells a translator that the result must be a poem in English. It does not tell her which of the original's claims to spend in order to get one.

[9] So the test I would put to a version is not how much of the original survives in it but whether it lets an English reader feel the place where the original will not come over. Aird's poem is the most beautiful of the three and the most closed: nothing in it points outward, and a reader can finish it without suspecting that anything is gone. Ozias's short line is an audible absence. The reader who trips on it has learned something true about Demeter that no amount of accuracy elsewhere would have taught her. A translation is at its best when the seam shows and the reader can see that a seam was necessary.

[1] Four lines of Ilka Demeter's "Field, November" have been turned into English three times in a century, by translators who agreed on almost nothing, and a reader who sets the versions side by side notices first that they are not even the same size. Fane's 1912 quatrain runs to thirty-eight syllables. Aird's 1968 version runs to twenty-six and breaks into five lines. Ozias, in 2004, gives twenty-nine across four. None of the three is careless. No two of them are wrong in the same place.

[2] The Hungarian is a strict little machine. Demeter is working in a nine-syllable measure she used nowhere else, and she ends her second and fourth lines on der and kenyer - frost and bread - which rhyme fully, and which in the idiom of her region are also the two halves of a proverb about a hard winter. The rhyme is therefore not decoration. It is the poem's argument, compressed into a sound, and a translator who gives up the rhyme gives up the claim.

[3] Fane kept it. He gave himself hoar and store, pulled the syntax around into an inversion no English speaker has produced since, and delivered a quatrain that rhymes, scans, and sounds like a hymnal. It is easy, and it has become customary, to be condescending about this version. But Fane is the only one of the three who registers that the poem is built on a sound, and the stiffness of his English is the price of a structural fact the other two let go. What he paid it with was the ordinary voice. Demeter's diction in the Hungarian is flat, domestic, almost without literary furniture; Fane's is furniture throughout.

[4] Aird, writing at the height of the vogue for plainness, produced what most anthologies still print. She recovered the ordinary voice exactly - in her hands the poem sounds like a woman saying something across a kitchen table - and she recovered it by letting the rhyme go, and the nine-syllable measure with it, and the proverb that lived inside the rhyme. That is a trade and not an oversight. Aird knew what was in those two words; she says so in a letter to her editor, and she says she could not have both.

[5] Ozias tried to hold both and had to pay somewhere else. He found an English pair, rime and crust, that carries the frost and the bread and is idiomatic enough not to creak; and to get those two words into rhyming position he compressed his third line until a clause fell out of it, the clause in which Demeter calls the field idegen, a stranger. Word for word, the Ozias version is the least complete of the three. Everything he preserved was bought with that missing clause, and he prints the Hungarian underneath so that the purchase can be seen.

[6] Talk about translation goes wrong, I think, at the point where it pictures a poem crossing from one language into another and arriving with some percentage of itself intact. The traffic between two languages is not carriage. It is negotiation, and every version is a settlement with terms. Fane's terms are rhyme over voice. Aird's are voice over structure. Ozias pays in clauses. These are not three attempts at one target with three error rates; they are three different bargains, and a reader is owed the terms of the one in front of her.

[7] There is a fact that ought to embarrass anyone who wants to rank the three by fidelity, and it is that Demeter was herself a translator. Her Hungarian versions of the French poet Aline Ricour, published in 1934, are not faithful by any standard she would have been graded on. She moves stanzas. She supplies an image where the French has an abstraction. In one poem she changes the season. And in the note that prefaces the book she writes that she had tried to make in Hungarian the thing Ricour had made in French, and that doing so had obliged her to write different words. She did not take herself to be approximating an object. She took herself to be building a second one.

[8] The strongest case against all of this comes from the reader with no Hungarian, which is nearly every reader, and who quite reasonably wants a poem rather than a seminar on what a poem could not become. That reader is owed something whole, and I concede the priority: a version that does not work as an English poem has failed before any of the interesting questions arise, and Fane's, whatever it preserves, is now read for pleasure by almost nobody. But the concession settles less than it appears to settle. It tells a translator that the result must be a poem in English. It does not tell her which of the original's claims to spend in order to get one.

[9] So the test I would put to a version is not how much of the original survives in it but whether it lets an English reader feel the place where the original will not come over. Aird's poem is the most beautiful of the three and the most closed: nothing in it points outward, and a reader can finish it without suspecting that anything is gone. Ozias's short line is an audible absence. The reader who trips on it has learned something true about Demeter that no amount of accuracy elsewhere would have taught her. A translation is at its best when the seam shows and the reader can see that a seam was necessary.
